performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The first movement, Allegro non molto, of Winter, RV 297, from The Four Seasons. The strings depict shivering, stamping feet and chattering teeth, and between these passages the solo violin plays runs of demisemiquavers over the orchestra.

sections.label: A · Repeated notes, strings, bass upwards
sections.mNote: Repeated notes enter from the bass upwards; the violin adds trills.

sections.label: B · Violin broken-chord passage
sections.mNote: Rapid broken chords in the violin interrupt the shivering figure.

sections.label: A′ · Repeated notes in shorter values
sections.mNote: Repeated quavers shorten to semiquavers, then demisemiquavers.

sections.label: C · Solo violin runs and orchestral tutti
sections.mNote: The violin modulates from F minor towards E♭ major.

sections.label: A″ · Refrain in E♭ major
sections.mNote: The strings return with the refrain’s repeated notes.

sections.label: D · Solo violin, repeated semiquavers
sections.mNote: Repeated semiquavers take the solo back towards F minor.

sections.label: A′ · Stamping music in F minor
sections.mNote: The full strings repeat the stamping music to close.

cues.title: Opening, bars 1–11
cues.text: The 1725 sonnet opens with “Aggiacciato tremar trà nevi algenti” — “To shiver, frozen, among icy snows.” Repeated string notes build upwards from the bass. The solo violin joins with a trill on each short note.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, letter A; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 1–11: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351. The sonnets were published anonymously with Op. 8.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Solo violin, “Orrido Vento”
cues.text: “Al Severo Spirar d’orrido Vento” — “In the harsh breath of a dreadful wind.” The solo violin plays demisemiquavers in broken chords and descending scales. Short orchestral passages bring back the shivering figure.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter B; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 12–18, solo marked Orrido Vento: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Stamping feet, bars 22–26
cues.text: “Correr battendo i piedi ogni momento” — “To run, stamping one’s feet at every moment.” Vivaldi set the repeated notes closer together. The semiquavers break into short bursts of demisemiquavers.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter C; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 20–26; the stamping inscription begins halfway through bar 22: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Charles de Brosses on Vivaldi, 1739
cues.text: Charles de Brosses wrote from Venice in 1739: “Vivaldi has become one of my intimate friends, to sell me concertos very dear.” The old man, he added, had a prodigious fury for composing, boasting he could write a concerto, with all its parts, faster than a copyist could copy one.
cues.evidence: Charles de Brosses, letter XVIII to M. de Blancey, 29 August (1739), Lettres familières écrites d’Italie (ed. Hippolyte Babou, Poulet-Malassis et de Broise, 1858, vol. 1, pp. 141–148): “Vivaldi s’est fait de mes amis intimes, pour me vendre des concertos bien chers”, “une furie de composition prodigieuse”, and “plus promptement qu’un copiste ne le pourroit copier”; translation ours. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettres_famili%C3%A8res_%C3%A9crites_d%E2%80%99Italie_T.1/%C3%80_M._DE_BLANCEY._%E2%80%94_Suite_du_s%C3%A9jour_%C3%A0_Venise

cues.title: Solo violin, “Batter li denti”
cues.text: “E pel Soverchio gel batter i denti” — “And to chatter one’s teeth from the excessive frost.” The solo violin repeats short notes under the words Batter li denti. The repeated notes continue while the harmony passes through A♭ major and C minor towards F minor.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter D; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 47–56; harmonic route in José Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final ritornello
cues.text: The full strings take over in F minor for the final ritornello (bars 56–63). Vivaldi brings back the stamping part of the refrain, with its rapid repeated notes, and carries it to the final cadence.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 56–63, final ritornello; its use of the stamping music is identified at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From F minor to C minor
transitions.from: A · Repeated notes, strings, bass upwards
transitions.how: The shivering passage moves from F minor to C minor. The solo violin begins the wind on C, leaping an octave and then running through the notes of a C-minor chord. The orchestra interrupts with short returns of the shivering rhythm. The marking stays Allegro non molto.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 9–18; key change discussed at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: Refrain to the stamping-feet episode
transitions.to: A′ · Repeated notes in shorter values
transitions.how: The wind returns to F minor and the full strings resume the repeated-note refrain. At bar 20 the violin changes its short quavers to semiquavers on F. Demisemiquaver bursts then interrupt the semiquaver pulse under the inscription about running and stamping feet.

transitions.title: Solo violin episode, F minor to E♭ major
transitions.from: A′ · Repeated notes in shorter values
transitions.to: C · Solo violin runs and orchestral tutti
transitions.how: In bars 26–38 the stamping string chords stop and the solo violin enters in F minor. Its demisemiquavers circle F, E♮ and G, then climb higher. Beneath it the orchestra keeps the shivering figure, then breaks in with bursts marked winds as the episode moves towards E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 26–38; orchestral wind interruptions and E♭-major destination described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: Refrain returns in E♭ major
transitions.from: C · Solo violin runs and orchestral tutti
transitions.how: The solo episode reaches E♭ major. The full strings bring back the repeated-note refrain in that key, including its semiquaver version. Vivaldi kept the denser stamping figures back for the final return in F minor.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 38–44; the refrain’s contents are identified at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: Solo episode to the final tutti
transitions.how: The soloist leaves the E♭-major refrain for another rapid passage. At bar 47 the repeated semiquavers carry the inscription Batter li denti. The episode moves through A♭ major and C minor and reaches F minor for the last tutti.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 44–56; harmonic itinerary at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

transitions.title: Return to F minor and the stamping music
transitions.to: A′ · Stamping music in F minor
transitions.how: The solo episode reaches F minor, and the full strings take up the stamping music. Rapid repeated notes alternate with broken chords. The final refrain is built on this denser part of the earlier tutti and continues with it to the F-minor cadence.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 56–63; final ritornello described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/01.php.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: I. Allegro non molto; opening staggered entries, solo passages and ritornellos. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: Low repeated notes open the movement and build up the texture.
The viola joins the repeated-note texture; timing is approximate.
The second violin part adds another layer; timing is approximate.
The upper violin parts, including the soloist’s trills, complete the texture.
Wind solo with brief orchestral interruptions; the full strings do not play continuously.
The refrain develops its stamping figure.
The next solo passage begins while the orchestral upper strings rest.
Orchestral wind interruptions enter the solo-led passage.
The refrain returns in E♭ major.
The soloist begins the later episode before the chattering figure.
Repeated semiquavers depict the chattering teeth.
Full strings take the final stamping refrain.

voices: Organ and cello bass line (not realised continuo)

composer.epithet: Venetian composer of concertos for the women of the Pietà and operas for the city’s theatres, who wrote a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 Antonio Vivaldi, a twenty-five-year-old Venetian, was ordained priest in March and became a violin teacher in September. He had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and went on helping with his career long after the son had become famous. In Venice Antonio was known as il prete rosso, the red priest. He worked in the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year. In 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 they took him back.
